summary: Two processes on one SQLite file: no busy_timeout, deferred transactions, and caches that never hear each other
detail: From the v0.5.0 review (TODO #8, Reported). Nothing sets PRAGMA busy_timeout, and writes use db.transaction() (deferred; .immediate() is the fix), so the first write after another process's read lock fails SQLITE_BUSY at once and a valid write 500s. And the in-memory document cache is per process with no invalidation, so two server processes on one file serve divergent state. Either document one process per file as a hard rule (the skill's feature table now says 'one per file') or give SQLite a change channel like the Postgres listener. Repro: two `bun` processes calling registerDocs on the same file, one holding a read transaction while the other writes.
note: 2026-09-24: carried from TODO.md #8; still open after round 2.

summary: A whole-row replace means two things: the JSON file replaces the row, SQLite and Postgres merge the fields sent
detail: From the second review pass (TODO A3). `replace /coll/id` with a partial value drops the missing fields on the JSON-file backend (RFC 6902) and merges them on SQLite and Postgres. The skill's 'Backends side by side' table now says so ('send it whole'). Either registerDoc merges at depth 2 to match, or the SQL backends replace. Repro: scratchpad/delta-reviewer/parity.ts, case 'whole-row replace with partial value'.
note: 2026-09-24: carried from TODO.md A3; documented, not unified.

summary: The server handles a socket's messages concurrently, so a signed-in client that doesn't use onConnect still races its own authenticate
detail: Round 2 fixed the reconnect freeze on the client (connectWs(url, { onConnect }) runs before any doc (re)opens). Without the hook, one thing remains: createWs's message handler is async and not serialised per socket, so an `open` sent right after `authenticate` can be handled first and 401 (the 'variant B' of scratchpad/delta-reviewer/reconnect-auth.ts, re-run as scratchpad/round2-delta-fixer/reconnect-auth.ts). Per-socket serialisation would block slow handlers (recompute, registerMethod), so make it opt-in if it is done.
note: 2026-09-24: the server half of D2; client half fixed in round 2. 2026-09-25 review: the second half (a re-open's 401 only logged, never retried) moved to #17, the same frozen-document symptom; lowered to low, since onConnect is the documented fix for the rest.

summary: SQLite has no auth: no gate, no owns, every socket may open every document of a prefix
detail: D9 from round 1. registerDocs takes no DeltaAuth, and open/delta never ask who is writing, so the SQLite tier cannot be multi-user safe without hand-written ws.on shims. The skill now says 'no auth' in the feature table and the SQLite quick start. A minimal fit with round 2's Postgres design: registerDocs(..., { auth, owns }) with the same default-deny as docTypeFromDef.
note: 2026-09-24: round-2 proposal; documented, not built. 2026-09-25: history too: SQLite's `history` answers any caller about any document, where the CHANGELOG says 'to whoever may open it'.

summary: SQLite documents have no list mode, and a root row can only be made over the wire by an implied document
detail: D9 / dogfood A3, A4, P5. `defineDoc('todos:', { root: 'todos' })` opened as `todos:` looks for the row id '' and answers 404 (the message now says why). The shape of a document therefore differs from Postgres ({todos} there, {lists, todos} here). implied: true covers creating the root on first write; seeding with SQL covers the rest. Postgres also needs a raw INSERT for a single-mode root row.
note: 2026-09-24: round-2 proposal; the 404 names the rule now.

summary: SQLite opens and broadcasts carry valid_from and valid_to; Postgres strips them
detail: Seen while writing the SQLite quick start (scratchpad/round2-delta-fixer/sqlite-quickstart.ts): the open snapshot's rows and every echo include the temporal storage columns, which then sit in the client's doc.data. Postgres runs _delta_strip_temporal on both. inverseOf already strips them (withoutStorage). Stripping them on SQLite too would make the document shape the same on both SQL backends.

summary: Two validateOps: SQLite's (types, root fields) and Postgres's (a subset, which the listener never calls)
detail: CLAUDE.md used to say validateOps lived in src/schema.ts, shared; it does not. sqlite.ts has the full one; postgres/schema.ts exports a smaller one for callers, and the Postgres listener relies on delta_apply's checks instead (round 2 added unknown and required fields there). One shared validator is the DRY answer, but Postgres list-mode documents address rows on the root collection where SQLite treats /<root>/<x> as a root field, so it needs the document's mode.

summary: The CLI is not agent-safe yet: no in-band token, watch never exits, only ops that land on a ledger come back
detail: Round 1 (delta.md §4, §5). An auth-enabled server can't be reached (the token must not go in the URL, so it needs an in-band `call authenticate` first: --token / DELTA_TOKEN); `watch` never exits, so a Bash tool call hangs (--count N, --for 5s); `delta` returns only {ack}, not the ops as applied (--print-ops); and there is no offline `validate` or server `describe`. These come before an MCP wrapper.
note: 2026-09-24: round-2 proposal. 2026-09-25 review: `delta` now prints the whole answer (ops, inverse, version, entry on a ledger backend); still missing: a token, a watch that exits, and offline validate / describe.

summary: The test surface is not shared: mockClient and sendAndAwait are not in the package, and the pointer vectors are one test file's, not data eta can run
detail: Consumers can't import mockClient/sendAndAwait (tests/ is not in the package; the skill now says so). And the one pointer grammar is pinned by VECTORS in tests/postgres-pointer.test.ts, run through splitPath and _delta_split_path; as a JSON fixture (wire-vectors.json) eta's json-pointer.ts could run the same cases without a dependency (proposal-final.md §4). The team's larger idea is backend conformance stories (who does what, who sees it) run against JSON, SQLite and Postgres; tests/create-row.test.ts and tests/error-codes.test.ts are the first two. The walk planners too (was #21): planWalk and _delta_walk_plan are one rule in two languages with no shared cases; a list of { entry: { ops, inverse }, current, expected: { ops, conflict } } run through both would pin them as the pointer vectors pin the two parsers. And eta's side of the wire law (was eta #22): the same vectors, as data, run by eta.

summary: An onConnect that calls through DI (call("authenticate", params) with no client) deadlocks: the client never connects, and says nothing
detail: onConnect runs before `ready` resolves, and only the client it is given skips `ready`. `connectWs(url, { onConnect: () => call("authenticate", { token }) })` with `provide(WS, ...)` sends through inject(WS), which waits for `ready`, which waits for onConnect: `connected` stays false for good, no document opens, and nothing is logged. The docs show the right form (`(ws) => call(..., ws)`), but it is one missing argument. Repro: scratchpad/round2-delta-reviewer-2/onconnect-di.ts (HANG, connected: false). Options: a log.warn when onConnect has not settled after a few seconds, or a request made from inside onConnect's async context going straight out.
note: 2026-09-24: found by the round-2 review; not fixed.

summary: SQLite applies a batch's field writes after its adds and removes, so a batch that changes a row and then removes it is a 404
detail: applyOps in sqlite.ts collects field replaces (and whole-row replaces) into rowFieldBatches and writes them after the loop over adds and removes. `[replace /items/y/name, remove /items/y]` fails 'Row not found: items/y' (the JSON file and Postgres apply it in order), and a batch's ops are not applied in the order sent. Found writing the net-change walk test (222f3ae): the SQLite case uses remove-then-add instead. Either apply in order, or say in the skill's side-by-side table that a SQLite batch writes fields last.
note: 2026-09-24: found by the round-2 review; low.

summary: No law per document: nothing proves a copy equals a fresh read from the tables after every change
detail: epsilon's proveLaw drove a document type's ops over the real wire and checked, after every echo, that the client's copy deep-equals a fresh composition from the tables, undo and mirrors included, naming the likely defect when not. delta has no such harness, so a fan-out, cascade or echo that diverges from the tables is found by an app, if at all. A `proveLaw(doc, drive)` for both backends, over a socket, with undo and every document holding the rows checked.
note: 2026-09-25: from the survey of every completeness check from dzql to eta. 2026-09-25 review: lowered to low: a test harness, not something a user hits. 2026-09-25: tests/helpers/path.ts asks the law at the end of every case, on every backend; what is still open is a law run over generated writes, not only the cases.

summary: An included grandchild whose parent collection is not included loads differently on the two backends
detail: Found while fixing #2. `_delta_load_collection` walks up to a parent the document does not include and loads its children anyway: `user:` with include ["memberships"], memberships under teams (no parent), loads every team's memberships on Postgres (teams in full) and none on SQLite (loadCollection returns [] for an ancestor with no parent that is not included, which is what rowInScope and tests/write-scope.test.ts 'cascadeOn is not scope' expect). A parented ancestor that is not included (root -> a -> b, include ["b"]) is walked on both, but SQLite's rowInScope needs the parent in the document's cache, so such a b row is loaded and never fanned out. Needs a decision: refuse an include whose parent chain leaves the document (at registerDocs / generateSql, where the schema is known), or walk it the same everywhere.
note: 2026-09-25: found fixing #2; not changed (the Postgres side is the framework SQL contract).

summary: The fan-out's questions left open when #28 closed: its cost at scale, RLS, and custom DocTypes
detail: From #28's review. (c) Cost: a scoped or list-mode definition, or an unparented collection, makes _delta_holders scan the opened names of its prefix (starts_with over _delta_versions) and ask _delta_doc_holds of each; measure at allertons' scale (261 venues, 14.7k sites, 1,350 occasions) and index or bound it. (b) _delta_versions is never pruned, so a document opened once is told for ever: cheap, but decide whether the listener should say which names are open. (d) RLS: the holders are worked out as the writer (app.user_id); a parent row the writer cannot see hides a document its owner can: decide whether the walk is SECURITY DEFINER. (e) A DocType registered from TypeScript is not in _delta_docs, so the database cannot tell it: say so, or give it a way in.

summary: An implied document is the JSON file's and SQLite's alone: Postgres ignores implied, and a name-keyed one (room:attic) cannot hold a serial id
detail: Found writing the path (one app on every backend). implied: true opens a document before its root row exists and makes the row on the first write; SQLite and the JSON file do it, Postgres answers 404. And the idiom names the root by text (room:attic, session:<token>), which Postgres's serial ids cannot hold. An app that uses it cannot move along the path unchanged: either Postgres gains implied for serial ids, or the name-keyed idiom is kept to documents that never move (sessions), and said so.

summary: A recompute custom document is Postgres's alone
detail: Found writing the path. defineCustomDoc's membership mode (query + matches) runs on both; recompute (a whole-document view re-evaluated on any watched write) only on Postgres. An app that uses one cannot start on SQLite or the JSON file.

summary: `replace /<root>/<id>` is a row replace on Postgres but a 400 on SQLite
detail: Through a single document, `replace /courses/1 {...}` (the root row by its collection and id, as a list document would say it) is taken on Postgres as the whole-row replace of that row, and refused on SQLite, which only knows the root as `/courses`. Decide the one answer (probably accept both spellings of the root, as the id is known) and make both agree, with a shared case.
note: 2026-09-27: found by the team fixing n43-n47

summary: A field replace then a remove of the same row in one write succeeds on Postgres but is a 404 on SQLite
detail: SQLite applies a batch's field writes after its adds and removes (see n20), so `[replace /drinks/3/name, remove /drinks/3]` removes the row first and then fails the replace with 404; Postgres applies the ops in order and succeeds. Related to n20; fix both by applying ops in order on SQLite, with a shared case.
note: 2026-09-27: found by the team fixing n43-n47

summary: A json-scoped list's writer isn't told of an add whose name is a JSON string or object, though a reopen has the row (SQLite)
detail: For names like "5" (quoted), {}, [] or "a", SQLite's meets() compared the name's text with the decoded JSON, so the writer wasn't told; for 5.0, " 5", 1e0 the writer was told but a reopen lacked the row; Postgres is self-consistent for all of them. #45's change (meets reads the name through scopeValue) may have closed this: check on its merge, and close or narrow this item with a shared case.

summary: Undo of one write that renames a document's root and then removes it conflicts on every backend
detail: A batch [replace /courses/name, remove /courses] through course:1 records an inverse whose walk finds a conflict at /courses, so that write can never be undone; the same on SQLite, the JSON file and PGlite. The inverse should put the root back as it was before the batch.
